title: Sidewalk Area: Street Tree Guidance and References
summary: Page 77 of the LADOT Complete Streets Design Guide, in Section 4 Sidewalk Area. It gives street tree guidance on mature height, spacing from street lights, pedestrian lights and utility poles, planting size, trunk diameter, height and clearance to building elements. It lists references including UFD guidelines and BOE Standard Plans S-456-1 and S-450 and the Bureau of Street Services tree permits.
description:
Text page: Printed page 77 of the Complete Streets Design Guide, section header 4. SIDEWALK AREA. The page has two columns of text. The left column is a bulleted list of street tree guidance. The right column is a References list placed above a photograph.

Photograph 1 (right column): A sidewalk with a mature street tree whose canopy covers the walkway, with pedestrians, seated people and parked cars beside it. No caption.

Photographs 2 and 3 (lower half, side by side across the page): A row of young street trees planted in a landscaped parkway strip between the curb and the sidewalk. The left photo shows a blue street light pole, a parked car and a yellow fire hydrant beside the curb. The right photo shows the same tree row along a sidewalk with a pedestrian and a red painted curb. No captions.

The page ends with a Back to Table of Contents link and the page number 77.
notes:
Guidance bullets (left column):
1. Mature height: no limits or maximums, but should be appropriate and complement roadway scale, use and land uses.
2. Spacing from other elements: Trees with a mature canopy diameter of 30 feet or less may be 20 feet from street lights. Trees may be 10 feet from pedestrian lights if their canopies are pruned up 2 feet above the lights. Trees may be 10 feet from utility poles if canopies are pruned to allow access on the poles. In certain locations, smaller clearances may provide greater flexibility in tree spacing and allow for a more complete tree canopy. These clearances may be used with Urban Forestry Department (UFD) approval.
3. Tree size at planting: Arterials, 36-inch box recommended (not currently standard). Non-arterials, 24-inch box.
4. Trunk diameter: Arterials, 2 to 2.5 inches. Non-arterials, 1 to 1.5 inches.
5. Height: recommended Arterials, 14'. Non-arterials, 10'.
6. Adequate clear space should be provided between trees and awnings, canopies, balconies and signs so they will not come into conflict through normal growth or require excessive pruning to remediate such conflicts.

References (right column):
- Urban Forestry Department (UFD) Residential Parkway Landscaping Guidelines
- UFD Street Tree Selection Guide
- Bureau of Engineering (BOE) Standard Plan S-456-1: Tree well, root barrier and planting
- BOE Standard Plan S-450
- Current permitting through Bureau of Street Services: Tree Root Prune Permits, Tree Prune Permits, Tree Removal Permits, Tree Planting Permits

title: Bicycle Racks: Rack Characteristics, Policy and Amenity Zone Placement
summary: Page 89 of the LADOT Complete Streets Design Guide, Section 4 Sidewalk Area. It finishes the list of rack characteristics, states the inverted-U rack as the standard and then gives amenity zone placement. Racks parallel to the curb need at least 24 inches from the curbline (preferably 36 inches beside a travel lane), 5 feet of clearance along a line, 90 inches between curbside racks and 5 feet from other street furniture.
description:
Text page: Printed page 89, section header 4. SIDEWALK AREA, running header Complete Streets Design Guide. Two columns. The left column carries the end of a bulleted list of rack characteristics (two sub-bullets with diamond markers) followed by three policy bullets. The right column carries the heading Location and Placement of Bicycle Racks, the sub-heading Amenity Zone, one paragraph and two bullets.

Photograph (lower center, across both columns): Several bicycles locked to racks at the curb in front of a planted tree bed on a sidewalk, with a street and traffic in the background and a pedestrian at the right. Caption: Wide sidewalk areas afford opportunities to consolidate multiple racks in groups.

The page ends with a Back to Table of Contents link and the page number 89.
notes:
Left column:
(Continuation of the rack characteristics list from the previous page; each item is introduced by an earlier lead-in not on this sheet.)
- Have mounting hardware that can be unscrewed with common tools.
- Requires the bicyclist to lift their bicycle onto the rack.
1. While the inverted-U design is the accepted standard in Los Angeles for bicycle parking in the public right-of-way, other rack designs may be accepted for use at the discretion of LADOT and approval of the Department of Public Works. The installation of creatively designed racks can provide a public art amenity. These should be encouraged, especially in pedestrian-oriented districts.
2. In addition, property owners are encouraged to install bicycle racks in the frontage zone near building entrances (after receiving the required conditional permit from the Bureau of Engineering (BOE)) or on private property near building entrances.
3. New development projects must provide a minimum number of bicycle parking spaces per the Los Angeles Bicycle Parking Ordinance, section 12.21.AA16 of the Municipal Code.

Right column, Location and Placement of Bicycle Racks, Amenity Zone:
4. Bicycle racks that are parallel to the curb should be a minimum of 24 inches from the curbline to allow for access to parked vehicles and provide adequate space for cyclists to maneuver. To provide added safety for bicyclists, when fronting a curbside vehicular travel lane racks should be set back further, preferably at least 36 inches from the curbline.
5. The rack should allow a minimum of 5 feet of clearance when placed parallel to the roadway (along a single line), measured from center of base plate to center of base plate. In areas with curbside vehicular parking, a rack oriented parallel to the curbline must be a minimum of 90 inches from another curbside rack to ensure pedestrians have clear access to and from the curb parking between two parked parallel bicycles (BOE S-671 Standard Plan).
6. The rack should maintain 5 feet of clearance from other street furniture. Other street furniture includes but is not limited to: parking meters, trees, tree wells, newspaper racks, light poles, sign poles, telephone poles, utility meters, benches, mailboxes, fire hydrants and trash cans.
Photo caption: Wide sidewalk areas afford opportunities to consolidate multiple racks in groups.

title: Bicycle Racks: Frontage Zone, Flex Zone, Other Discussion and References
summary: Page 90 of the LADOT Complete Streets Design Guide, Section 4 Sidewalk Area, continuing the bicycle rack placement guidance. It covers racks near bus stops and hydrants, frontage zone orientation and spacing (30 inches from the structure, 60 inches side by side), flex zone curb extensions, and other discussion on meters, repair stations and compliance. References include APBP, NACTO, BOE Standard Plan S-671 and the 2013 Bicycle Parking Ordinance.
description:
Text page: Printed page 90, section header 4. SIDEWALK AREA, running header Complete Streets Design Guide. The left column continues the amenity zone bullet and then gives Frontage Zone and Flex Zone Curb Extensions guidance. The right column has Other Discussion (three paragraphs) and a References list.

Photograph (lower center): A bicycle hung by its front wheel on a black bike repair stand at the curb of a street, with parked cars and a lot in the background. Caption: Bike repair stations are a valuable public convenience for bicycle riders.

The page ends with the page number 90 and a Back to Table of Contents link.
notes:
Left column (continues Amenity Zone):
1. A bicycle rack should not be installed in a bus stop zone, taxi zone or loading zone. A rack should not be installed near a fire hydrant or near handicap-accessible parking.

Frontage Zone:
2. In the frontage zone, bicycle racks can be placed perpendicular, angled or parallel to a building or property frontage. Perpendicular or angled parking should be provided if space permits. These orientations allow for better-accessible clustered parking.
3. Racks located parallel to the property line should be placed at least 30" from the structure. When racks are placed side by side, each rack should be spaced at least 60" from one another in order to accommodate both rider and bicycle in the aisle.

Flex Zone - Curb Extensions:
4. Bicycle racks located on mid-block curb extensions should comply with all guidelines stated above for racks located in the amenity zone. Bicycle racks should generally not be located on corner bulbouts near intersections because they hinder visibility for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorists.

Other Discussion (right column):
5. Los Angeles code does not currently allow decommissioned parking meters to be retrofitted to accommodate bicycle parking, although LADOT has completed pilot retrofit projects. This is common practice in many other localities and should be considered in Los Angeles.
6. Bike repair stations are a valuable convenience for cyclists. These should be located in strategic locations with high bicycle traffic, ideally placed adjacent to clustered parking facilities. To ensure security and safety, they should be placed in a secure part of the street that is highly visible and well lit.
7. The current placement of bicycle racks should be checked for compliance with standards. Racks that are not in compliance should be relocated, as designated by LADOT under guidance by the above guidelines as well as those in Standard Plan S-671.

References:
- APBP Bicycle Parking Guidelines
- NACTO Urban Bikeway Design Guide
- BOE Standard Plan S-671
- 2013 Bicycle Parking Ordinance (LAMC Ord. No. 182386)
Photo caption: Bike repair stations are a valuable public convenience for bicycle riders.

title: Bicycle Corrals: Placement, Other Discussion and References
summary: Page 134 of the LADOT Complete Streets Design Guide, Section 5 Roadways, Bicycle Enhancements. It gives bicycle corral siting rules: a red curb zone is allowed if standard clearances are met, with at least 25 feet from a fire hydrant, 30 feet from intersection departure and 50 feet from intersection approach. It also describes the Bicycle Friendly Business Program and lists references including Standard Plan S-671.
description:
Text page: Printed page 134, section header 5. ROADWAYS, running header Complete Streets Design Guide, tab label Bicycle Enhancements. Two columns. The left column has two bullets of corral placement guidance followed by an Other Discussion heading with two bullets. The right column has a References list.

Photograph (lower center, across both columns): A storefront on York Boulevard with inverted-U bicycle racks at the curb holding several parked bicycles, a street tree, a sign post, a traffic signal pole and a curb painted red near the corner. Caption: York Boulevard, Highland Park.

The page ends with the page number 134 and a Back to Table of Contents link.
notes:
Placement bullets:
1. Corrals can be located in a red curb zone as long as standard clearances are met. There should be at least a 25 foot clearance from a fire hydrant.
2. Bicycle corrals should be located at least 30 feet from intersection departure and 50 feet from intersection approach.

Other Discussion:
3. LADOT should consider developing a standard plan for the placement and design features of bicycle corrals, including striping, signage, dimensioning and other elements.
4. Bicycle corrals are part of LADOT's Bicycle Friendly Business Program, a public-private partnership that serves local stakeholders, business owners or community partners that are interested in increasing bicycle friendliness in their community by hosting a bicycle corral outside of their establishment. LADOT pays for the corral, site design and installation in the public right-of-way, while the requesting party agrees to become a maintenance partner that ensures the corral's cleanliness and upkeep.

References:
- LADOT Bike Blog: ladotbikeblog.wordpress.com/bike-corrals/
- LADOT Bicycle Friendly Business Program http://ladotbikeblog.wordpress.com/bicycle-friendly-business-program/
- Standard Plan: S-671 Bicycle Rack
Photo caption: York Boulevard, Highland Park

title: Peak-Hour Bus Lane: Design Guidance, Additional Discussion and References
summary: Page 137 of the LADOT Complete Streets Design Guide, Section 5 Roadways. It gives design guidance for peak-hour curbside bus lanes, pointing to LADOT standard plan S-487 for Exclusive Bus Lane Markings, and describes the Wilshire Boulevard BRT peak-hour lanes (7.7 miles, weekdays 7 to 9 am and 4 to 7 pm). A photo shows a bus lane with ONLY legend and a red curb.
description:
Text page: Printed page 137, section header 5. ROADWAYS, running header Complete Streets Design Guide, tab label Bicycle Enhancements. Two columns. The left column is the Design Guidance bullet list, which continues on the right with the last bullet, then Additional Discussion and References.

Photograph (lower center, across both columns): A street in downtown Los Angeles with a curbside bus lane. White pavement legend text reading ONLY and part of another word are visible in the lane, with dashed white lane lines, a bus ahead in the lane, a gray SUV in the adjacent lane, and a red painted curb along the sidewalk with a street tree. Caption: Red paint on the curb emphasizes the lane's exclusive dedication to bus use.

The page ends with a Back to Table of Contents link and the page number 137.
notes:
Design Guidance:
1. Peak-hour bus lanes should be installed with the appropriate parking signage and pavement markings (See City of Los Angeles' Department of Transportation standard plan S-487 for Exclusive Bus Lane Markings for further detail).
2. At intersections, right turning movements by other motorists and bicyclists can be facilitated by marking dashed lines at the intersection approach. If buses traveling in the lane experience significant delays, right turns at select intersections may need to be prohibited.
3. Transit signal prioritization should be given to buses operating in these lanes.
4. Bus pads should be installed at stops to prevent street warping.
5. Alternatively, a peak-hour bus lane can be offset, meaning the bus only lane is located one lane away from the curb (See Section 5.8 "Offset Bus Lane").
6. Peak-hour bus lanes may also be designed as shared bike-bus lanes (See Section 5.6 "Shared Bike/Bus Lane").
7. Red paint should be considered as a supplemental treatment used to delineate and reinforce the lane for bus use only.

Additional Discussion:
8. Starting in 2013, the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (Metro), in partnership with the City of Los Angeles, implemented curbside peak-hour bus lanes on a 7.7-mile segment of Wilshire Blvd as part of their Wilshire Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Project. Overall, the project aims to improve bus passenger travel times, service reliability and ridership along the corridor. The bus lanes are operational on weekdays from 7 am to 9 am and 4 pm to 7 pm. In addition, bicyclists are also allowed on these lanes during the peak period.

References:
- FTA Bus Lanes http://www.fta.dot.gov/12351_4358.html
- Effective Bus-Only Lanes http://nacto.org/docs/usdg/effective_bus_only_lanes_kiesling.pdf
- The City of Los Angeles' Department of Transportation currently has a standard plan (S-487) for Exclusive Bus Lane Markings.
Photo caption: Red paint on the curb emphasizes the lane's exclusive dedication to bus use.

title: 5.9 Median Bus Lane / Busway
summary: Page 139 of the LADOT Complete Streets Design Guide, Section 5.9, Transit Enhancements. It defines median bus lanes and busways and lists their benefits, applications and design guidance, including a minimum median bus lane width of 11' and S-487 for Exclusive Bus Lane Markings. A NACTO rendering shows red median bus lanes with boarding islands and crosswalks.
description:
Text page: Printed page 139, section header 5. ROADWAYS, running header Complete Streets Design Guide, tab label Transit Enhancements. Heading 5.9 Median Bus Lane / Busway with an introductory paragraph spanning both columns. Below it, the left column has Benefits and Applications and the right column has Design Guidance.

Illustration (lower half, across both columns): A perspective rendering of an urban arterial with a center median bus lane colored red, with a white line between the two directions of bus travel, buses running in the median, a median boarding island with a shelter canopy, signalized crosswalks, median planting, signal poles and mast arms, general travel lanes with cars on the near side and street trees, sidewalks and pedestrians. Caption: Image courtesy of NACTO.

The page ends with a Back to Table of Contents link and the page number 139.
notes:
Introduction:
A median bus lane enhances transit service by providing a dedicated right-of-way for buses to run down the center of corridors. A median busway functions similarly to a median bus lane except that it provides a physical separation from vehicle traffic. For both of these facilities, passengers board and alight at station stops that are located on median boarding islands.

Benefits:
1. Minimizes conflicts with on-street curbside parking and vehicle turning movements.
2. Improves speed and reliability of transit by eliminating the need for buses to pull into bus stops and merge back into traffic.
3. Provides a lane for emergency vehicles to use in congested conditions.

Applications:
4. Median bus lanes should be considered on multi-lane arterial corridors where major transit service suffers from poor on-time performance, as a result of peak hour congestion.

Design Guidance:
5. The minimum width of a median bus lane should be 11'.
6. Median bus lanes should be installed with the appropriate pavement markings (See City of Los Angeles' Department of Transportation standard plan S-487 for Exclusive Bus Lane Markings for further detail).
7. Contiguous lanes that run in opposite directions should be separated by a solid single or double white stripe(s).
8. Median boarding islands should be placed in close proximity to safe, signalized crosswalks.
9. A median busway can be separated from other travel lanes using a curb strip or rumble strips.
Image caption: Image courtesy of NACTO.

title: Marked Uncontrolled Crosswalk Guidelines: A. Minimum Requirements
summary: Page 2 of 7 of LADOT's Marked Uncontrolled Crosswalk Guidelines (Rev. 10-05-2020), a fillable checklist of the five minimum requirements (a) through (e), each with Yes and No boxes and an All Satisfied check. The requirements cover pedestrian visibility from distance A in S-481.0, at least 20 pedestrian units in one hour, stopping sight distance to adjacent signals (table of 25 to 50 mph), no recurring queue spillback, and ADA curb ramps at both landings.
description:
Checklist page: Header Marked Uncontrolled Crosswalk Guidelines (Rev. 10-05-2020) at top left and Page 2 of 7 at top right. Section heading A. MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS. A two-column form: requirement text on the left and two check box columns headed YES and NO on the right. The first row is ALL SATISFIED? with one YES box and one NO box. Rows (a) through (e) each have their own YES and NO box, separated by thin dotted rules.

Row (a): Motorist visibility of pedestrians from distance A (shown in S-481.0) in both waiting areas, with the definition of the waiting areas. Row (b): Pedestrian volume of at least 20 units in one hour, with Note 1 and Note 2. Row (c): Distance to adjacent signalized intersections compared with stopping sight distance, with a table. Row (d): No queuing from downstream intersections spilling into the crosswalk location. Row (e): ADA curb ramps at both landings.

Table (inside row c): two columns, Posted or 85th Percentile Speed (mph) and Stopping Sight Distance (ft), with six rows. 25 mph, 153 ft. 30 mph, 195 ft. 35 mph, 242 ft. 40 mph, 294 ft. 45 mph, 350 ft. 50 mph, 415 ft.
notes:
A. Minimum requirements (each requirement has Yes and No check boxes, plus an All Satisfied? row with Yes and No boxes):
(a) Motorists in all approach lanes would be able to see pedestrians in both waiting areas for the proposed crosswalk from distance "A", as shown in S-481.0, during both daytime and nighttime conditions. The waiting areas are defined as follows: for locations with full-time parking lanes (where pedestrians are expected to wait to cross from within the parking lane): a point within the proposed crosswalk, 4 feet from the nearest curb face of the street being crossed near each landing. For locations without full-time parking lanes and with active travel lanes adjacent to the curb (where pedestrians are expected to wait to cross from the edge of the sidewalk): at the edge of the curb at each landing. Where additional nighttime visibility is required, the crosswalk may be authorized, contingent upon the installation of additional lighting.
(b) Pedestrian volume is at least 20 units during a one-hour period during any day of the week. All pedestrians crossing the major street mid-block, up to one block away from the proposed crossing, may be counted if they are expected to benefit and be served by the proposed crosswalk. Pedestrians crossing at the next upstream and downstream intersections may also be counted if those intersections do not feature a marked crosswalk. All pedestrians as noted above should be counted during one singular one-hour period.
Note 1: For both cases, children who appear to be under 13 years of age, elderly who appear to be over 64 years of age, persons pushing strollers, and disabled persons count as two (2) pedestrian units.
Note 2: Marked uncontrolled crosswalks can induce demand, particularly adjacent to attractors such as transit stops, schools, and commercial centers (ref. NACTO Urban Street Design Guide, Intersection Design Elements, Crosswalks and Crossings, Pages 110-111). A reduced threshold of pedestrian units can be used to satisfy this requirement if the projected pedestrian volume exceeds 20 units and such a projection is documented.
(c) The distance between the location and adjacent signalized intersections is greater than the minimum stopping sight distance based on the posted speed or 85th percentile speed, whichever is greater. Stopping sight distance is shown in the following table: 25 mph, 153 ft. 30 mph, 195 ft. 35 mph, 242 ft. 40 mph, 294 ft. 45 mph, 350 ft. 50 mph, 415 ft.
(d) There is no documented history or field observations of queuing from downstream intersections that regularly spills into the location of the proposed crosswalk. If such queuing is observed or documented, it must be resolved prior to, or in conjunction with, the installation of the proposed crosswalk.
(e) ADA-accessible curb ramps are present at both landings of the proposed crosswalk, or will be installed as part of the installation of the crosswalk. If such curb ramps are not technically feasible, this requirement is waived, contingent upon a documented determination from the Department on Disability that a marked crosswalk at the proposed location without curb ramps would be a "reasonable accommodation."

title: Typical Layout for Activated Pedestrian Warning Device
summary: LADOT typical layout for a pedestrian-activated flashing yellow beacon at a marked crosswalk, with advance signing, shark-teeth yield markings and PED XING pavement legends. It shows W11-2, R1-5, R9-3a, R9-3b, R62E(CA) PPB and W16-7p signs, 20 ft mast arms and a 30 ft dimension, plus a Detail A of the 36 inch by 42 inch W11-2 (mod) sign with W16 (mod) arrows. Timing diagrams show the alternating three-pulse flash pattern of Beacon One and Beacon Two, with 60 flash periods per minute.
description:
Plan view (typical layout): A roadway shown vertically with the centerline and lane lines. The plan is drawn with a break line (zigzag across the roadway) at the top and bottom, so the approach lengths are not to scale. A marked crosswalk with high-visibility bar markings crosses the street near the middle of the sheet, with curb returns of side streets on each side. The roadway width between curbs is dimensioned W. On each side of the crosswalk a 30' dimension is shown from the crosswalk to the line of yield triangles (shark teeth) on the approach, drawn on the right side of the sheet.

On each approach, two white triangle rows (yield line) sit before the crosswalk, the centerline is a double line that shifts (a curved offset) to form a left turn lane with a turn arrow, and PED XING legends are painted in the approach lanes near the break lines. At each end of the crosswalk, curbside signs are called out on posts: W11-2 (advance pedestrian crossing sign, shown at the top and bottom of the layout as a dot and callout), R1-5 (yield here to pedestrians sign) with R9-3a's and R9-3b's, R1-1 (stop sign at the side street), and R62E(CA) PPB (pedestrian push button sign). Each crosswalk end has W11-2's and W16-7p's on a pole assembly with a 20' Mastarm carrying two flashing yellow beacons (labeled FL.Y) over the roadway, one set on the near side and one set on the far side of the crosswalk. Detail "A" is called out at the beacon pole assemblies. A symbol at the top left of the sheet identifies the beacon symbol as a flashing beacon activated by pedestrian push button.

Detail A: A sign drawing, 36" wide by 42" tall, with a black walking pedestrian symbol and two downward diagonal arrows at the bottom corners on a white field with a black border. Labeled W11-2 (mod) for the sign and W16 (mod) for the arrows.

Beacon One timing diagram: Pulse intensity against time from 0 to 1.0 sec. Three pulses are shown between 0 and 0.5 sec, each 0.1 sec on and 0.1 sec off (duty cycle dimension On 0.1, Off 0.1), at 0 to 0.1, 0.2 to 0.3 and 0.4 to 0.5 sec. No pulse from 0.5 to 1.0 sec.

Beacon Two timing diagram: Pulse intensity against time from 0 to 1.0 sec. No pulse from 0 to 0.5 sec, then three pulses at about 0.5 to 0.6, 0.7 to 0.8 and 0.9 to 1.0 sec, so the pulses of Beacon Two fill the pause of Beacon One.

Title block: Title Typical Layout for Activated Pedestrian Warning Device, City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation, Drawing No. S-55.0, sheet 1 of 1, approved June 24, 2010 by Rita L. Robinson, General Manager. Drawn by EC, dated 6-10-10.
notes:
Legend: Flashing beacon activated by pedestrian push button (beacon symbol at top left).
Notes:
1. The flash pattern utilizes LED heads and a Model 2070 controller. There are 60 flash periods per minute. The flash period for each beacon includes three pulses within 0.5 seconds and a pause of 0.5 seconds. The pulses of one beacon alternate with the pause of the other beacon, as shown below.
2. Flash length is W/3.5 seconds and retimes with each call. (W is the roadway width dimension shown on the plan.)
3. See S-481.0 for required advance signing, pavement marking, and red curb.
4. At school crossings, school related signs and pavement markings shall be used in place of those shown hereon, as per S-481.0.
Sign and drawing labels on the plan: W11-2, W11-2(mod), W16(mod), W11-2's and W16-7p's, R1-1, R1-5, R9-3a's, R9-3b's, R62E(CA) PPB, 20' Mastarm, Detail "A", FL.Y (flashing yellow).
Dimensions: sign 36" by 42", 30' from crosswalk to yield line, W roadway width, 20' mast arm. Timing: On 0.1 sec, Off 0.1 sec.

title: Special Detector Applications: Bus Priority Detection
summary: Sheet 5 of 6 of LADOT standard S-75.0 showing plan views of bus priority detection loops at signalized intersections. Three views are given: with an arterial cross street, with a minor cross street and on a divided street. Loops B1 to B4 are set 15 ft upstream of the bus zone or placed 3 ft from the ends of the intersection area, and each is wired to a PB3 pull box. The boxed callouts 1 to 5 refer to notes that are not printed on this sheet.
description:
Sheet: Three plan views stacked on one sheet, each showing a signalized intersection drawn with a rectangle containing a circled S, left turn arrows, crosswalk lines, lane lines and curb returns.

View 1, Bus Priority Detection with An Arterial Cross Street: A multilane street approaches the intersection from the left and also from the right. On the left approach, a long bus loop B2 (labeled BUS LOOP) runs across the through lane next to the bus zone (a thick black line at the curb marked BUS ZONE). The loop sits 15' upstream of the near end of the bus zone, and has a 3' dimension at each end to the curb face and the pavement edge. A lead-in runs from the loop to a PB3 pull box (black square) at the south curb, with an existing interconnect conduit (EXIST. I/C, dash-dot line) running along the south side behind the curb. Boxed callouts 1 and 4 point at the pull box. On the right approach, bus loop B1 is 15' from the bus zone (BUS ZONE shown at the south curb) with a 3' dimension at the top end. It connects to a PB3 at the north curb. A dash-dot conduit runs to a second PB3 at the curb return and continues to a PB3 at the far corner. Boxed callouts 1 and 3 are shown at these pull boxes.

View 2, Bus Priority Detection with A Minor Cross Street: The minor street crosses the major street at the center. Bus loop B1 is drawn as a long oval inside the intersection rectangle with a 3' dimension at each end from the edge of the intersection area. The detector lead-in is shown running to a signal pole (small rectangle) with a pair of loop symbols (callouts 1 and 5), with the word OR indicating two possible connection routes, one toward a pole on the left and another through a PB3 pull box on the right marked ALTERNATIVE CONNECTION SEE NOTE 5. SEE NOTE 4 and BUS LOOP are labeled at B1.

View 3, Bus Priority Detection on A Divided Street: A street with a raised median (stippled fill) and a left turn pocket on each side of the intersection. Along the left approach, bus loops B4 (upstream, 15' from the bus zone) and B3 (near the intersection) flank the BUS ZONE, each at a PB3 pull box, with a dash-dot conduit labeled with callout 3 between them. The loop spans the lane between the curb and the median with dimension 3' TYP. at each end. On the right approach, the mirror arrangement uses loops B2 (near the intersection) and B1 (upstream, 15' from the bus zone) with PB3 pull boxes, 3' TYP. dimensions and callouts 1, 2 and 3. An extra PB3 sits at the corner return with a dashed conduit.

Title block: Special Detector Applications, City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation, circled sheet number 5 over 6, Drawing No. S-75.0.
notes: No numbered notes are printed on this sheet. The boxed callouts 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 on the plan refer to notes shown on another sheet of S-75.0. Labels on the plan: BUS ZONE, BUS LOOP, B1, B2, B3, B4, PB3 (pull box), EXIST. I/C (existing interconnect), S (signalized intersection), OR, ALTERNATIVE CONNECTION SEE NOTE 5, SEE NOTE 4. Dimensions: 15' from the bus zone to each bus loop, 3' at the ends of the loops, 3' TYP. across the lane in the divided street view.

title: Visibility Nomograph for Standard Visor Head
summary: Sheet 4 of 11 of LADOT standard S-85.0, a nomograph for a standard visor signal head. Place the center line along the assumed head alignment to see whether the 50 percent lens visibility lines (27 degrees each side, 54 degrees total) cross the limit line of a conflicting approach. The 0 percent visibility lines are at 45 degrees each side.
description:
Nomograph (single view): A symmetrical fan of lines starting at a dot (the signal head position) at the top and opening downward, with a vertical dashed center line labeled Center of Signal Head Alignment. A heavy arrow near the upper right points down, showing the viewing direction.

Angles: 27 degrees on each side of the center line to the lines labeled 50% Visibility of Lens, and 45 degrees on each side to the lines labeled 0% Visibility of Lens. A 54 degree dimension arc spans between the two 50% lines. The shaded wedge between the 50% lines is labeled Not to be seen by conflicting approach.

Heading: Visibility Nomograph for Standard Visor Head. Instruction text below it: Place the line for Center of Signal Head Alignment along assumed alignment of head. Determine conformance with restricted visibility to conflicting approaches.

Title block: Application of Visibility-Limited Traffic Signal Heads, City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation, circled sheet 4 over 11, Drawing No. S-85.0.
notes:
1. Place the line for "Center of Signal Head Alignment" along assumed alignment of head. Determine conformance with restricted visibility to conflicting approaches.
Labels and angles: 0% Visibility of Lens at 45 degrees each side of the center line. 50% Visibility of Lens at 27 degrees each side of the center line (54 degrees total). The shaded area is Not to be seen by conflicting approach.

title: Visibility Nomograph for Beveled Visor Head
summary: Sheet 5 of 11 of LADOT standard S-85.0, a nomograph for a beveled visor signal head. The 50 percent lens visibility lines are 27 degrees on the left of the center line and 13 degrees on the right (40 degrees total), and the 0 percent lines are 45 degrees left and 24 degrees right. The shaded wedge between the 50 percent lines is not to be seen by a conflicting approach.
description:

title: Lateral Visibility: Beveled Visor Application (Arden St. and Diagonal St.)
summary: Sheet 9 of 11 of LADOT standard S-85.0, an example of using the visibility nomograph at the Arden Street and Diagonal Street intersection. A standard head (Angle A, 54 degrees) aimed at Arden Street would be seen too easily from Diagonal Street. A left-beveled visor (Angle B, 40 degrees) keeps the shading off the Diagonal Street limit line and restricts lateral visibility adequately.
description:
Plan view: An angled intersection of Arden St. (running vertically, labeled at the top and continuing to the bottom) and Diagonal St. (running diagonally from upper left to lower right, labeled at the right). The plan is drawn with the page rotated so the streets run at an angle. Lane lines, dashed lane dividers, double center lines, left turn arrows and curb returns are shown on all legs. Limit lines (stop lines) are drawn across each approach.

Signal head and nomograph overlay: A dot at the corner near the top marks the signal head, with a line labeled Center of Signal Head Alignment running down along Arden Street toward the approach, and an arrow at the head. Two shaded fans are overlaid from the head. The wider fan is marked A (54 degrees) and the narrower fan marked B (40 degrees), each with an arc dimension. Fan A crosses the limit line on Diagonal Street. Fan B stays clear of that limit line.

Text blocks (right side): A = 54 degrees: Angle of 50% lens visibility of a standard signal head. The signal head shown is intended for Arden Street motorists. However, it can be seen too easily by Diagonal Street motorists, since the Angle A shading crosses that limit line. B = 40 degrees: Angle of 50% lens visibility of a left-beveled visor signal head. Since the Angle B shading does not cross the limit line on Diagonal Street a left-beveled visor would adequately restrict lateral visibility.

Caption under the plan: Lateral Visibility: Beveled Visor Application, followed by two small head symbols (an arrow and a beveled visor block, shown for the left or right beveled head).

Title block: Application of Visibility-Limited Traffic Signal Heads, City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation, circled sheet 9 over 11, Drawing No. S-85.0.
notes:

B = 40 degrees. Angle of 50% lens visibility of a left-beveled visor signal head. Since the Angle B shading does not cross the limit line on Diagonal Street a left-beveled visor would adequately restrict lateral visibility.
Other labels: Arden St., Diagonal St., Center of Signal Head Alignment, Lateral Visibility: Beveled Visor Application.

title: Street Name Sign Posting
summary: Sheet 1 of 4 of LADOT standard S-221.3. A schematic plan of a street grid shows where street name signs (for example W Ave., C St., B St., X Ave., A St., Y Ave.) are posted at corners, including a curved street and a U-shaped street. The four notes require signs close to the near-right B.C. or the extension of the near left, ahead of obstructions, on existing posts or electroliers where practical, and treat parallel roadways with different names as separate streets.
description:
Plan view (schematic, no scale): A block of generic streets used to show posting locations. Vertical streets are labeled "C" STREET, "B" STREET and "A" STREET. Horizontal streets are labeled "W" AVENUE (across the top), "X" AVENUE (left center) and "Y" AVENUE (a U-shaped street that curves around a rounded end at the right). A curved street at the upper left bends from "C" Street toward B Street and X Avenue. Curbs are drawn as double lines with rounded corner returns.

Sign symbols: Each street name sign is a small rectangle with the street name in it, joined by a curved leader to a post symbol (a short bar with a dot) placed at a corner. Names shown include C St., W Ave., B St., X Ave., A St. and Y Ave. Posts are at the near-right corner of each approach. At some corners two names appear on the same post, for example W Ave. with A St., and B St. with A St. At the bottom a post carries B St. and A St. side by side, with the word OR beside an alternative post location below it.

Title block: Street Name Sign Posting, City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation, circled sheet 1 over 4, Drawing No. S-221.3. Approved January 21, 2005 for Wayne K. Tonda, General Manager. Drawn by M.T., Pr. T.E. TJ.
notes:
Note:
1. All signs shall be posted as close to the near-right B.C. or the extension of the near left as is practical.
2. Post sign in advance of obstructions where encountered.
3. Existing sign posts and/or electroliers shall be used to post street name signs wherever practical.
4. Two parallel roadways with different street names (for example, Huntington Drive North and Huntington Drive) shall be treated as two different streets for sign posting purposes.

title: Typical Major Highway Striping Treatments: Major Highways (Prior to 11-10-99), 100' R/W, 80' Roadway
summary: Sheet 1 of 5 of LADOT standard S-401.0 (major highways, prior to 11-10-99, 100 ft right of way with 80 ft roadway). Two plan views show a two-way left turn lane ending at a signalized intersection, one open-ended with a 30 ft minimum to a critical driveway and one closed-ended with a 70 ft minimum, with lane widths and 60 ft or 80 ft reversals. Nine notes give minimum left turn pocket lengths (100 ft at major and secondary highways, 60 ft at collectors, 40 ft at local streets), 10 ft wide channelization and bike lane width limits.
description:
Heading: MAJOR HIGHWAYS (PRIOR TO 11-10-99), 100' R/W - 80' ROADWAY. Two plan views stacked one above the other, each a four-lane or six-lane section approaching a signalized intersection at the right (circled S). In both, the right of way is 100' wide, the roadway is 80' wide (40' each side of the center) and each side has a 10' sidewalk or parkway strip outside the roadway. Stopping prohibition arrows are drawn along the curb beyond the roadway.

First drawing (open-ended two-way left turn lane): Roadway with dashed lane lines and a center two-way left turn lane. A critical driveway (box with an X) is shown on the lower curb with a 30' MIN. dimension. Near the intersection the center lane transitions with a reverse curve into a single left turn pocket with a left turn arrow, with a 60' OR 80' reversal dimension. Stacked lane width strings appear at both ends of the view: 23' to 24' for the two lanes on one side, 10' to 12' for the center lane, 11' and 11' for the next lanes and 12' to 13' for the curb lane (partly legible, the small 11' and 12' figures are crowded).

Second drawing (closed-ended two-way left turn lane): Roadway with a critical driveway on the lower curb and a 70' MIN. dimension. The center lane transitions at both ends with tapers, labeled TAPER at top and bottom, and a [illegible]" YELLOW diagonal marking. A reversal length of 100' TO 120' is dimensioned. At the intersection end, two opposing left turn pockets with arrows meet the signal. Lane widths on the left side: 12' to 13', 11', 11', 10' to 12' center, 11', 11', 12' to 13'. At the intersection end: 11', 10', 10', 11' on each side with 9' and 9' for the two left turn pockets. The 40' dimension to each side of the center and the 100' overall is shown on the right.

Title block: Typical Major Highway Striping Treatments, City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation, circled sheet 1 over 5, Drawing No. S-401.0. Approved February 24, 2006 for Frances T. Banerjee, Interim General Manager. Drawn by M.T., T.E. T.C.
notes:
NOTES:
1. Selection of length of left turn pocket lane depends on demand, spacing between intersections and location of critical driveways to be served by two-way left turn lanes (2WLTL). The desirable length at signalized intersections is at least 40' of storage per vehicle per signal cycle averaged during the peak hour. However, this desirable length often may not be feasible. Minimum lengths at signalized intersections on highways with continuous median channelization are: 100' at major highways. 100' at secondary highways. 60' at collector streets. 40' at local streets. Minimum pocket lengths for major highways without continuous median channelization may be less than the above, depending on turning volumes and parking impacts.
2. In general, 10' wide left turn channelization should be used. However a 12-foot median should be used if large vehicles are a significant portion of turning vehicles.
3. Utilize 60' reversals for posted speed limits of 35 MPH and less, and 80' reversals for posted speed limits of 40 MPH and greater. A 40' minimum reversal may be used in exceptional situations for critical driveways.
4. Selection of an open-ended (as shown in first drawing) versus closed ended (as shown in second drawing) 2WLTL is dependent, in part, on the proximity of a critical driveway to be served by a 2WLTL. Minimum distances to critical driveways are shown.
5. The painted reversal for a single left turn lane may be eliminated at a signalized intersection on a selective basis if spillover is recurrent and if it is not feasible to lengthen the left-turn pocket.
6. For new raised median installations, the width of the island should be limited to 8' to allow wider adjacent through lanes.
7. The 4' wide island adjacent to the left turn lane should be removed, where feasible, so as to avoid left turn lane offsets which reduce left turn driver visibility of approaching through vehicles. Where an island adjacent to the left-turn lane is proposed, or is to be retained, protected left-turn phasing shall be considered. See Standard Plan S-497.0.
8. Third through lanes should be installed when conditions so justify. Right turn only lanes may be installed instead of the third through lane, as appropriate.
9. Bike lanes with all day parking may be installed in place of a curb lane or right turn lane where the width is 13' or greater (or 12' in selected cases).
Drawing labels: CRITICAL DRIVEWAY, 30' MIN., 70' MIN., STOPPING PROHIBITION, TAPER, 60' OR 80', 100' TO 120', [illegible]" YELLOW.

Stalls are marked with 4 inch white lines at 45 degrees and 8 inch tall white MOTORCYCLE stencils, with optional K71 bollards or candlestick delineators in end boxes, R32F(CA) Sign A with arrows and Sign B Motorcycle Parking Only. A table gives overall dimension A for 2 to 6 stalls (12 ft to 30 ft).

A parking meter sits 20" from the face of curb and 3' from the end of the red curb. The 19' parallel stall length is dimensioned. Then a hatched end box 2' wide containing three circled K symbols (K71 bollards or candlestick delineators) with 4" white lines at 45 degrees. The box is followed by a 3' red curb (R/C) section. A second end box with three K symbols, 2' wide and 3' deep, closes the run at the cross street end near the curb return. Signs: Sign 'A' (R/A) right arrow and Sign 'A' (L/A) left arrow are both R32F (CA), a green on white sign reading 2 HOUR PARKING 8AM-6PM with MOTORCYCLE PARKING ONLY and an arrow. Sign 'B' is a black and white sign reading MOTORCYCLE PARKING ONLY, 6" x 8" min.
